1. On Thursday, 17 December 1953, while flying near Hassleholm, Sweden, Captain Ulf Christiernsson sighted an "unknown" object. The following is the translation of a newspaper account of the incident:

"The chief pilot of Transair, Capt. Ulf Christiernsson, and his crew chief, Olle Johansson, had a strange meeting over Hassleholm at 1437 hours Thursday. A shining metal spherical elliptical object came toward them traveling in the opposite direction from their machine at an estimated speed of sound and approximately 600 meters below their DC-3, which was on its way from Bulltofta to Bromma. It was visible six to seven seconds; Capt. Christiernsson, who had good silhouette recognition, stated that what he saw was something absolutely new, possibly an unmanned robot.

"The Transair plane was automatic controls when the meeting occurred. Capt. Christiernsson did not have time for any measures other than to report to Bulltofta and the Defense Staff, which later sent out the following communique:

"'The air crew of a civil aircraft observed on Thursday at 1437 hours over the area of Hassleholm an unknown object moving in the opposite direction from the airplane. The object was observed for six to seven seconds. At that time and altitude the weather was clear. Because of the low lying cloud formations the object is not thought to have been seen from the ground. The Defense Staff does not know of any Swedish plane that was in that area at the time in question. An investigation is being conducted.'

"Previously I have been extremely skeptical about all the stories of mysterious objects -- called flying saucers -- that have been seen at diverse points, said the Captain. Now I don't know exactly what to think; but it did seem to me that we had seen a robot of some kind. When I first caught sight of the object, which like us was in the civil air corridor, I thought it was a jet. We had, however, received no word that any such thing was on the way.

"The object came toward us at what I would say was the speed of sound; we were flying at an altitude of approximately 2,150 meters and the object was around 600 meters below us. It was going in a southwesterly direction and disappeared after six or seven seconds.

"The object had a strong metal shine; the crew chief, Johansson, who could see it longer than I, thought it was almost phosphorescent. The flying weather was excellent above the clouds, which were at an altitude of about 1500 meters, and the sun was shining brightly. The object was proceeding just above the clouds.

"The first silhouette I got diagonally from the right was narrow. When it was nearly directly under us, however, I saw that it was nearly round, just slightly elliptical.

"The object, which could definitely not have been a meteor, gave off no waste gases or condensation traces.

"Was I afraid? No, but curious, very curious, concluded Captain Christiernsson.

"Christiernsson has seen just about everything in aviation and has very good silhouette recognition. From 1942 to 1946 he was a volunteer serving in

AIR INTELLIGENCE REQUIREMENTS
MEMORANDUM NUMBER 4

UNCONVENTIONAL AIRCRAFT

PART I - GENERAL

1. PURPOSE

The purpose of this memorandum is twofold:

a. To enunciate continuing Air Force requirements for information pertaining to sightings of unconventional aircraft and unidentified flying objects, including the so-called "Flying Discs."

b. To establish procedures for reporting such information.

2. RESCISSION

Department of the Army Collection Memorandum Number 7, dated 21 January 1948, and letter, CSGID 425.1, dated 25 March 1948, both subject as above, which have been transferred to Air Force agencies for action, are herewith superseded.

3. REPORTING

a. General

(1) As complete an answer to the requirements enunciated in Part II, as may be procurable, should be dispatched by means of electrical transmission immediately after sightings.

(2) Supplementary reports should be forwarded as available by the most expeditious means consistent with the importance of the information reported.

b. Major Air Commands (Overseas) and Air Attaches

(1) Initial and supplementary cabled reports will be transmitted to the Director of Intelligence, Headquarters United States Air Force. Cables will contain the phase, "Pass to COMGENAMC WRIGHT-PATTERSON AFB, DAYTON, OHIO, ATTN: MCIAXO-3."

C9-4892, AF
RESTRICTED

RESTRICTED

(2) Supplementary written reports, prepared on AF Form 112, will be forwarded to the Director of Intelligence, Headquarters United States Air Force.

(3) Commanding General, Air Materiel Command is authorized direct contact with major Air Commands (overseas) and organizations under their control in connection with the development of information on this subject.

c. Major Air Commands (ZI)

(1) Reports will be forwarded direct to the Commanding General, Air Materiel Command, Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Dayton, Ohio, Attn: MCIAXO-3 by installations receiving information pertaining to the requirements enunciated in Part II.

(2) Copies of such reports may be supplied the Command Headquarters of the installation concerned.

(3) A copy of all reports sent to Air Materiel Command in accordance with these instructions will be forwarded at the same time to the Director of Intelligence, Headquarters United States Air Force.

(4) Written reports will be submitted on AF Form 112.

(5) Commanding General, Air Materiel Command is authorized direct contact with major Air Commands (ZI) and organizations under their control in connection with the development of information on this subject.

d. Non-Air Force Agencies

(1) Addressees other than those of the United States Air Force are requested to forward reports direct to the Commanding General, Air Materiel Command, Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Dayton, Ohio, Attn: MCIAXO-3.

(2) In order to reduce the time factor involved in transmission of this type of information it is requested that, wherever communications facilities permit, subordinate elements be authorized to communicate reports direct to the Commanding General, Air Materiel Command.

PART II - REQUIREMENTS

General

1. Date of sighting.

2. Time of sighting (zonal by 24 hr. clock).

3. Where sighted (observer's position):

a. Ground

(1) City, town.

(2) Distance and direction from city or town, road, intersection, etc.

(3) From building (story), yard, etc.

(4) Map coordinates (if feasible) showing latitude and longitude.

(1) Latitude and longitude.

(2) Proximity to land. (Name city, country, etc.)

4. Number of objects.

5. Observable celestial phenomena or planets that may account for the sighting. (Local facilities or organizations which follow such celestial phenomena should be consulted for such information.)

d. Size.

(2) Size as it appeared from observer's view. (Compared to known object)

9. Direction of flight.

10. Tactics or maneuvers.

Vertical ascent or descent, horizontal, oscillating, fluttering, evasive, aggressive, erratic, etc.

11. Evidence of exhaust.

a. Color of smoke.

b. Length and width.

(1) Sound.

c. Degree of fatigue and duration of flight at time of sighting in cases where observer is airborne.
9. Witnesses.
a. Addressees.
b. Occupation.
c. Reliability.
10. Comments of interrogator regarding the intelligence and character of person interrogated.
Relative to Radar Sightings
1. Re radars operating on ground.
a. Observations of range, speed, altitude and size of target.
b. Did target executive any turns? If so, what angle (180°), etc. and what radius of turn. If radius of turn is not observable, how long did the target stay in the turn and what was its speed?
c. Note particularly any separation of distant target into several targets upon approach. Track all if possible.
2. If airborne when object sighted.
a. Were there any radar inductions or extra noise on radio circuits?
b. Give estimates of size, speed, maneuvers, etc.

2. Winds aloft report.

3. Local flight schedules of commercial, private and military aircraft flying in vicinity at the time. (Check Canadian activity if close to that border.)
4. Possible releases of testing devices in vicinity sent aloft by Ordnance, Navy, Air Force, Army, Weather Units, Research Organizations or any other.
5. If object contacted earth, obtain soil samples within and without depression or spot where object landed (and then presumably departed) for purpose of making comparison of soils.
6. If object came sufficiently near other aircraft or known objects check surfaces with Geiger counters for possible radioactivity. Make comparisons with other unaffected aircraft objects, etc.
7. Obtain photographs (or original negatives) where available; if not, secure sketches of:
a. Object.
b. Surrounding terrain where observed.
c. Place where it contacted earth (if this happened).
d. Maneuvers.
e. Formation if objects were more than two.
8. Secure signed statement.
9. Obtain fragments or physical evidence where possible.
10. Was any radio antenna to be observed, i.e., (any projections or extentions that might presumably be construed as such).

General

1. Date of sighting.

2. Time of sighting (zonal by 24 hr. clock).

3. Where sighted (observer's position):

a. Ground

(1) City, town.

(2) Distance and direction from city or town, road, intersection, etc.

(3) From building (story), yard, etc.

(4) Map coordinates (if feasible) showing latitude and longitude.

b. Air

(1) Type aircraft, speed, altitude, direction of flight.

(2) Distance and direction from city, town or known landmark.

(3) Clock position of object from observer's aircraft.

(4) Latitude and longitude.

c. Sea

(1) Latitude and longitude.

(2) Proximity to land. (Name city, country, etc.)

4. Number of objects.

Formation type (if any), sketch if possible.

5. Observable celestial phenomena or planets that may account for the sighting. (Local facilities or organizations which follow such celestial phenomena should be consulted for such information.)

6. Distance of object from observer.

a. Laterally or horizontally.

b. Angle of elevation from horizon.

c. Altitude.

7. Time in sight.

8. Appearance of object.

a. Color.

b. Shape. (Sketch if possible)

c. Apparent construction. (Of what material or substance)

d. Size.

(1) Estimated size.

(2) Size as it appeared from observer's view. (Compared to known object)

9. Direction of flight.

10. Tactics or maneuvers.

Vertical ascent or descent, horizontal, oscillating, fluttering, evasive, aggressive, erratic, etc.

11. Evidence of exhaust.

a. Color of smoke.

b. Length and width.

c. Odor (if any).

d. Rate of evaporation.

e. Does trail vary with sound? (spurts)

12. Effect on clouds.

a. Opened path thru clouds.

b. Forced cloud or mists.

c. Reflected on cloud.

d. Showed thru cloud.

13. Lights.

a. Reflected or attached.

b. Luminous

c. Blinked on and off in relation to speed.

14. Support

a. Wings.

b. Aerodynamic list of fuselage.

c. Vertical jet.

d. Rotating cylinder or cone.

e. Aerostatic lift (balloon or dirigible).

15. Propulsion.

a. Propeller or jet.

b. Rotor.

c. Aerodynamic vanes (flapping or oscillating) (Katz Mayer effect).

16. Control and stability.

a. Fins

b. Stabilizers (horizontal or vertical).

(1) Size.

(2) Shape.

(3) Location.

17. Air ducts.

a. Slots.

b. Duct openings.

18. Speed - M.P.H.

19. Sound.

a. Continuous whine or buzz.

b. Roar, whistle, whoosh.

c. Intermittent.

20. Manner of disappearance.

a. Explode.

(1) Possibility of fragments.

(2) Other physical evidence.

b. Faded from view.

c. Disappeared behind obstacle.

Relative to the Observer

1. Name of observer.

2. Address.

3. Occupation.

4. Place of business.

a. Employer or employee.

5. Pertinent hobbies.

a. Is observer amateur astronomer, pilot, engineer, etc.

6. Ability to determine:

a. Color.

b. Speed of moving objects.

c. Size at distance.

a. Sources.

(1) Neighbors.

(2) Police Dept.

(3) FBI records.

(4) Employer.

a. Sightings in general.

b. How attention was drawn to object(s).

(1) Sound.

(2) Motion.

(3) Glint of light.

9. Witnesses.

a. Addressees.

b. Occupation.

c. Reliability.

10. Comments of interrogator regarding the intelligence and character of person interrogated.

1. Re radars operating on ground.

a. Observations of range, speed, altitude and size of target.

DECEMBER 16, 1963

DIARY NOTE

Subject: SA-5

1. NASA provides bimonthly launch briefings to the Department of State on all NASA launchings scheduled for the following two-month period.

2. The SA-5 launch was flagged at the briefing of October 23 because of the large weight expected to be put in orbit and re-enter. No objection was registered by the Department of State.

3. The following day, October 24, Mr. Frutkin called Dr. Golovin to recommend that Dr. Weisner be briefed on the SA-5. Golovin was to arrange a meeting for this purpose. A request for a briefing was received from Dr. Steininger of Dr. Weisner's staff on December 9, 1963, and he was briefing that day by Capt. Holcomb (NASA).

4. Prior to the initial briefing, NASA had taken two principal precautions to reduce the total weight of fragments that might return: (1) 13,000 lbs. of sand were substituted for the ballast originally programmed (lead and iron); (2) the Jupiter nose cone was roughed up so that it would burn up during reentry.

5. At Department of State request, a second briefing on SA-5 was held on November 27. No objections were registered to the launching by Dr. Rollefson or his associates.

6. The facts which were presented in the briefing for Dr. Rollefson (subsequently revised as in Paragraph 7) are:

(a) There is a 95% probability that 2,800 lbs. of material will return to earth, a 75% probability that 4,600 lbs. will return and a 50% chance that 10,200 lbs. will return. The 2,800 lbs. would probably take the form of 30 to 39 fragments, consisting of six engines, three Titanium spheres and approximately 30 electronics packages. The difference between 2,800 lbs. figure and the 4,600 lbs. figure is in the Jupiter nose cone.

(b) It was stated that fragments would probably impact over an area between 2,170 and 2,500 miles long by 100 miles wide.

(c) None of the aluminum skin material is expected to survive reentry. Interior parts should therefore be exposed to heating during reentry. (Most fragments collected to date have been stainless steel pieces of Atlas skin).

(d) If 30 fragments reenter the atmosphere, the probability of a casulty is estimated at .0000179. If 39 pieces reenter, the probability is .0000232, or one casualty per 50,000 flights. A fragment is considered capable of inflicting injury or death if it hits with more than 58 foot pounds of kinetic energy.

(e) The nominal but uncertain lifetime projected for the satellite is 148 days. The vehicle is to be launched on a heading of 105°, with a 345 nautical mile apogee, 141 nautical mile perigee, 31.60 inclination and a 93.9 minute period.

(f) NASA has investigated the possibility of destructing the satellite in orbit. This does not appear feasible since any destruct short of vaporization would simply create more fragments of a lethal nature and increase the probabilities of a casualty. In order to vaporize the satellite, a nuclear charge would be required.

(g) At the current stage of engineering, it is not possible to provide retro-rocket and orientation systems to deorbit the satellite in open water. Some 18 months might be required for this and the solution would not be applicable to future required GEMINI missions.

(h) If the 13,000 lbs. of sand are subtracted, it is estimated that the vehicle will be of the approximate weight and size of Soviet vehicles which have already decayed. It is not known whether the Soviets have taken any precautions regarding fragments.

(i) A tracking beacon with a 45-day life has been placed on board the satellite to assist in monitoring it as closely as possible.

(j) It has been estimated that the reentry prospects here are not greatly different from Atlas reentries in which about 2,000 lbs. per flight are believed to have returned to earth.

RESPONSE TO QUERY
April 8, 1964
RE: Queries on Fragment Return from NASA Spacecraft or Space Vehicles
A much abbreviated guideline for RTQ has been provided by Mr. Scheer to various NASA officials who might be queried on this subject. The following more extensive responses are provided as background information to be used by the Administrator, Deputy Administrator, or Associate Administrator of NASA, in their judgment, in event of queries on the return of space vehicle fragments to the earth. It is suggested that the minimum information be used to satisfy a given query.
(A) FOR USE PRIOR TO AND AFTER A PARTICULAR LAUNCH BUT BEFORE ANY KNOWN IMPACT OF RETURNING FRAGMENTS:
1. Do fragments from (satellite X) pose a threat to life or property?
The probability that fragments from (satellite X) may cause damage or injury is remote. The probability of injury from natural meteorites is far greater.
2. a. What is the probability of impact?
There are many factors (e.g., time in orbit, atmospheric conditions, how the vehicle breaks up, dispersal pattern, etc.) involved and the calculations are extremely complex. We have assured ourselves, however, that the hazard is far less than many hazards encountered in everyday living.
b. What is the numerical probability that NASA has placed on this?
In the case of SA-5, it is one in 50,000 launches.
In the case of GT-1, it is one in 27,500 launches.
3. Has NASA taken steps to lessen the fragment problem?
Yes. NASA is actively engaged in minimizing it. For example, on the SA-5 satellite, NASA used 13,000 lbs. of harmless sand as ballast and roughed up the nosecone so that it would burn on reentry. On the GT-1 spacecraft, NASA bored large holes in the heat shield to assist burning during reentry. In addition to specific steps such as these, studies are underway to assist NASA in further coping with the overall reentry problem.

4. How many fragments may be expected to survive
From SA-5 - About 30
From GT-1 - About 55
5. If any fragments come down, where are they most likely to impact?
The small number of fragments surviving from any satellite will be dispersed over an area of thousands of square miles, most of which are likely to be oceans, seas, or other water surface.
6. Can the fragment problem be further decreased by exploding the orbiting element?
Explosion or destruct of the orbiting element could produce more fragments and, hence, increase the possibility of fragment impact.
7. If one were to be hit by a fragment, would it be lethal?
In the remote possibility that one were to be struck by a fragment, it might, depending upon area of body struck, be lethal. However, this is also true of being struck by a meteorite, and the possibility of being struck by a meteorite is greater than the possibility of being struck by a fragment from (satellite X). In fact, based on data provided through the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, the average number of meteorites over 2.2 lbs. which impact on the earth every year is estimated at 5628. This is many, many times greater than the total number of fragments to be expected from (satellite X). And, to date, there are no substantiated reports of injury from these meteorite impacts.
8. Meteorites are natural phenomena. Do you consider NASA justified in increasing the possibilities of a lethal impact, no matter how improbable?
Many human activities carry with them a demonstrable probability of casualty--flying, automobile driving, golfing during an electrical storm. But we do not stop driving, flying or golfing.

Very roughly, about the same as with Atlas reentries, from which there have been no casualties.

GUIDELINES
FOR INTERAGENCY HANDLING OF SPACE VEHICLE FRAGMENTS

1. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is designated as the agency responsible for receiving, [analyzing] and identifying [any] fragments, or suspected fragments of space vehicles of all types, including the contents thereof, which fall upon the territory of the United States or which otherwise come into its possession, except that the Department of Defense (DOD) is solely responsible for receiving and identifying fragments from vehicles launched by the DOD.

[2. NASA will turn over to the Department of Defense (DOD) as expeditiously as possible fragments which are readily identifiable as coming from space vehicles launched by the DOD.]

2. In the event NASA should come into possession of space fragments under the sole and exclusive responsibility of the DOD, NASA will deliver such fragments as expeditiously as possible to the DOD.

3. To insure prompt analysis for intelligence purposes, NASA and other U. S. Government agencies will [give] deliver to the DOD [and other responsible agencies access] as expeditously as possible and on a priority basis fragments (including whole vehicles) which are readily identifiable or suspect as coming from [space] vehicles launched from foreign countries. Such foreign fragments which come initially into possession of the DOD will be retained by DOD for analysis. Such analysis of foreign fragments will be completed expeditiously, and thereafter such fragments will [remain] be placed in the custody of NASA, pending final arrangements for their return to the launching country or for other appropriate disposition.

4. All other fragments will be retained by NASA pending agreement as to disposition.

5. NASA may continue to use the Smithsonian Institution for collection and analysis of fragments by contractual arrangements, and may also make appropriate arrangements for assistance with private agencies.

6. The DOD will notify NASA when deorbits are expected and when collection teams have been alerted to obtain the deorbiting fragments. Also, DOD will inform NASA of the results of such collection efforts whether successful or not.

7. The Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) will participate in the analysis of fragments of space vehicles which have utilized or transported, or are suspected of having utilized or transported, radioactive materials or special nuclear materials, and will exercise responsibility for special nuclear materials, in accordance with its statutory responsibility. In addition, the AEC will continue to make available to NASA and the DOD its special scientific capabilities.

8. The Department of State will provide policy guidance with respect to the final disposition of fragments from vehicles launched by foreign countries, or made available to the United States by foreign countries. The Department of State will provide assistance in the acquisition of fragments that fall on foreign territory.

9. NASA will serve as the focal point for the coordination and release of public information on fragments except for release of public information on fragments resulting from space vehicles launched by the DOD, which will be the responsibility of DOD.

GUIDELINES FOR INTERAGENCY HANDLING OF SPACE VEHICLE FRAGMENTS

1. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is designated as the agency responsible for receiving and identifying fragments, or suspected fragments of space vehicles of all types, including the contents thereof, which fall upon the territory of the United States or which otherwise come into its possession, except that the Department of Defense (DoD) is solely responsible for receiving and identifying fragments from vehicles launched by the DoD.

2. In the event NASA should come into possession of space fragments under the sole and exclusive responsibility of the DoD, NASA will deliver such fragments as expeditiously as possible to the DoD.

3. To insure prompt analysis for intelligence purposes, NASA and other U.S. Government agencies will deliver to the DoD as expeditiously as possible and on a priority basis fragments (including whole vehicles) which are readily identifiable or suspect as coming from vehicles launched from foreign countries. Such foreign fragments which come initially into possession of the DoD will be retained by DoD for analysis. Such analysis of foreign fragments will be completed expeditiously, and thereafter such fragments will be placed in the custody of NASA, pending final arrangements for their return to the launching country or for other appropriate disposition.

4. All other fragments will be retained by NASA pending agreement as to disposition.

5. NASA may continue to use the Smithsonian Institution for collection and analysis of fragments by contractual arrangements, and may also make appropriate arrangements for assistance with private agencies.

6. The DoD will notify NASA when deorbits are expected and when collection teams have been alerted to obtain the deorbiting fragments. Also, DoD will inform NASA of the results of such collection efforts whether successful or not.

I. DESCRIPTION OF SOURCE:
NAME: Raleigh Iyapanna
AGE: 14 Years
OCCUPATION: Elementary Student and Hunter
PLACE OF BIRTH: Little Diomede Island
II. RELIABILITY OF SOURCE:
This report was made on 6 October 1953 by, Raleigh Iyapanna, an Eskimo of Little Diomede Island. Every night during the week preceding the report he had maintained a watch on Big Diomede on his own initiative. ROY N. FOWLER states he believes the source to be fairly reliable and that the sighting of the light is possibly true. Source is in good health and has excellent eyesight.
III. REPORT OF SIGHTING:
At approximately 081025Z, the source observed a light on the southern tip of Big Diomede Island at an estimated height of 95 feet above sea level. He had been standing in the center of Little Diomede Village looking in the general direction of Big Diomede for about fifteen minutes prior to the sighting. Source observed the light when it appeared and watched it until it disappeared. The duration of the observation was estimated as lasting for several seconds. The light was described as being the size of a nickel coin held at arms length and about the same color as a burning match or dim flashlight. It was the sources opinion that the light came from a large flashlight or spotlight. Immediately after the light disappeared, the source ran to his house, about 25 yards away, and checked the time which was 1030Z. After checking the time he went back to his original position and continued to watch the area the light came from, however, the light did not reappear. For location of the light see Incl #1.
IV. WEATHER:
The night was dark but with no overcast, stars were clearly visible. Big Diomede Island was plainly outlined against the sky. Wind was from the north and estimated at about 5 MPH.
COMMENTS OF THE PREPARING OFFICER:
The location of the light is considered somewhat unusual because people have never been observed on that part of Big Diomede Island and because of the difficulty in reaching the location, particularly at night. If persons on Big Diomede wanted to signal to the Alaskan mainland, it could best be done from the southern tip of the island. From that point, the Alaskan coast from Wales

PREFACE

This preliminary transcript was made from voice tape recordings of the GT-4 flight crew debriefing conducted aboard the recovery ship, the USS Wasp, on June 9, 1965, and concluded at the Manned Spacecraft Center on June 12, 1965.

Although all the material contained in this transcript has been edited, the urgent need for the preliminary transcript by mission analysis personnel precluded a thorough editorial review prior to its publication. Errors in this transcript will be corrected as soon as possible and an official transcript will be published at a later date.

This document contains a transcript of the second part of the total debriefing. A preliminary transcript of the first part was published on June 16, 1965, and it contains the crew's description of the mission from an operational standpoint.

I know you and I have talked about this before but I think it's time--

McDivitt Okay. Mission Control System. I think the Mission Control on this flight was nothing short of excellent. We got all the information from the ground that we needed. We didn't get bothered by them unnecessarily, I don't believe.

14.0 TRAINING
14.1 Gemini Mission Simulator
McDivitt Okay. Over on Training now. The first topic is Gemini Mission Simulator and I think we touched lightly on this subject already. I think that it's an excellent trainer for procedures, system knowledge, launch, orbit, retrofire, reentry, and crew stations. I think the big problem with it is that it takes too long to turn it around. I think that we're fooling around with it too much, committing it to supporting other functions besides flight crew training. The simulator at the Cape was supposed to have been turned around at roughly two weeks after GT-3's launch, and about six weeks after the launch it still wasn't doing its job. When we went down there to start flying this completely checked-out simulator, we found that the launch phase worked, the orbit phase did not work, and the reentry phase did not work. After we got the orbit phase squared away, we found out that we kept losing reentry command system. We couldn't use Direct Control Mode in anything. We never did fly reentries

until shortly before the actual flight, at which time I think I had four total reentries about a week before the flight. Ed said he only flew four reentries on the simulator at the Cape in total. I probably flew fifteen, I would guess. That's total, so I think that the Gemini Mission Simulator fell down completely in preparing us for this flight.
White Well, not quite that bad, Jim.
McDivitt Well. Okay. We did get a lot of training from it, but I think that the turn-around time is completely inadequate. It made the job for the flight crews a lot tougher than it should have been.
White I don't know really what the problem is, but I think the people down there are working hard, and when things were working right, the training was outstanding. But, gee, there's just too much time when things weren't working right.
McDivitt That's right. I think that's a good point to make. People down at the Cape try very hard, and I don't think it's their problem. The program for the Cape Simulator was done here.

When it arrived down at the Cape, it was completely inadequate for the job, and I can't understand why that program wasn't checked out in better shape when it went down there.
White I think, also, they're caught as second-rate citizens as far as keeping their simulators up to date and getting the latest spacecraft changes in them. They seem to be way behind the spacecraft and indicated to me that the system did not permit them to update the simulator with the speed with which it ought to be updated to train the crews properly. The things that were characteristic of Gemini 4 were being incorporated in the simulator down there in the last two or three weeks when they should have been incorporated in the first two or three weeks after the changeover from GT-3 to GT-4. I think we just have to work on a faster processing of the changes in getting the pieces of equipment and the changes out to the simulator so that they can be incorporated in it. Once they got the changes down there, they got them incorporated into the simulator, seemed like, pretty

fast. As long as they weren't there, they
couldn't update that simulator. Another thing
that I'll, for the life of me, never understand
is where in the world the food boxes were for
that simulator down there. I think somebody
should explain just why it took about one month
to locate a pair of food boxes and put them on
the simulator down there. It was the only way
that we could actually work on the storage of
the pieces of equipment for our flight, and we
didn't get a chance to look at that until what

Reference (a) is a request from U. S. Air Force for the interpretation of movies of unidentified objects taken in Utah, 2 July 1952. Included among the enclosures are approximately 30 feet of processed, 16mm color motion picture film and a list of questions for guidance in determining the type of analysis desired. Reference (b) requested interpretation of additional movies taken in Montana, 1950. This report supercedes reference (c) and presents the test procedures and methods designed to answer the questions contained in enclosure 7 of reference (a). The results and analysis were performed by the Photogrammetry Division, Evaluation Department of this Center and do not necessarily represent the official attitude of the Department of the Navy or this Center. 2. Tests and Procedure. a. Plots. The film exposed in Utah is in very poor condition; dry, brittle, and with a tendency to break. After initial viewing, duplication of the film was performed in order to preserve the film. In the duplication process some color correction was made to permit better viewing of the objects. To prepare plots of the objects, a stop frame projector was rigidly mounted at a fixed distance from a finely-ground glass screen. The magnification was 22 times giving a format size of 14.2

Code O1/HWW/1bh J12 Serial: 0105 MAY 4 1953 CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION Subj: Interpretation of Movies of Unidentified Objects; progress report on A preliminary detailed study of the Utah film was made and it was decided that: a. Brightly colored spots of red and green lasting only one or two frames were not to be considered. b. Water spots could be detected easily and eliminated from the study. c. The color of the objects was fairly constant as blue-white. d. Size and luminosity of an object varied through-out the film. For convenience in interpretation, the film was divided into three parts, each part being considered an entity. Part I consisted of the footage taken at f8; Part II, the footage taken at f16 with a panning motion; and Part III, the footage taken at f16 during which the camera was held steady. Three definite groups of lights were observed throughout the film and plots were recorded as follows: TABLE I PLOTS OF POSITIONS Utah Parts Control Chart I II III Holding to lower group Not enclosed I II Holding to one object and azimuth of another 2 and 3 I Arbitrary 1/2 inch correction per frame for panning 4 III Holding to frame outline 5a and 5b I One image held to base line. Code O1/HWW/1bh J12 Serial: 0105 MAY 4 1953 CONFIDENTIAL SECURITY INFORMATION Subj: Interpretation of Movies of Unidentified Objects; progress report on b. Densitometric tests: Densitometric data were obtained with a Densichron, Model 2150 manufactured by the Welch Scientific Company. The Densichron has a scale range of 0-3. The procedure was to project each frame at approximately 22 times magnification onto a finely-grained-glass screen. The background (sky) was then measured at several places and the density set to 3.0 (variations in background densities were in the order of 0.02 and were regarded as uniform). A set of three readings were made of each of seven objects in Part I, and of the single object in Part III of the Utah Film. Readings were made of the entire Montana film. Enclosure (8a and 8b) are graphs of the density readings obtained of the two lower groups of objects in frames 1-129 of the Utah film. Enclosure (9) is a density graph of the single object (94 frames) in Part III. Enclosure (10) is a graph where six successive Densichron readings were averaged and advanced one reading each determinant. Of the Montana film, densities were plotted as above and are enclosures (11) and (12). The results of the density readings may be questioned in that these objects varied in size so that at the minimum sizes the densichron probe was measuring the entire object, and at the maximum size the probe was measuring only a portion of the objects. Because of this situation only the largest readings obtained by scanning the objects were used. It is understood that normal procedure would be to read the entire object. This was impossible with the equipment on hand. In addition the film, with which this investigation was conducted, is a duplicate of a copy. This raises the question as to whether the central portion of the objects were burnt out during the duplication processing. Density readings were made to compare the clear areas and the objects. It was found that the minimum difference is 0.4. This indicates that relative luminosity may still be obtained with the procedure used. Concurrent with the density readings, relative sizes of the objects were noted in order to correlate distance and luminosity. Enclosure (13) is a plot of the same object wherein the relationship of distance and luminosity can be detected in Utah film. 3. Answers to Questions. Answers keyed to the questions contained in enclosure (7) of reference (a) are hereby presented. They supercede those contained in reference (c) and present the final analysis as requested. 1. Analysis of the graph correlating luminosity and size indicate that as the luminosity of the objects increase, the size is larger also. This could be the effect of viewing directly, a reflecting surface. This is considered not probable because of the length of time they were viewed continuously on the film, approximately 90 seconds, and because of the angle through which they were photographed, approximately 60 degrees.

It is felt that if these images are reflective surfaces, blinking would occur during a period of 90 seconds while passing through an angle of 60 degrees when photographed at the rate of 16 frames per second. This premise would permit highly reflective balloons or spheroids to be a possibility. However, the velocity and acceleration computations (sub paragraph 8) rule this possibility out. It appears, therefore, that if these objects are a reflecting surface, they are of a design, speed, and power not commonly known. The velocity and acceleration attributed to the objects may be caused by light reflected off a highly reflective surface onto an atomospheric screen where a slight angular turn of the reflective surface would appear as high acceleration. This possibility is considered not probable because of the sun angle and atmospheric condition reported at the time of photography and because of the variations in luminosity which, under the above conditions would remain constant.

It is the majority opinion of the group conducting this analysis that these images are light sources. This will explain the non-blinking and variations in luminosity - but not the velocity or acceleration factors. In either case, light source or reflective surface, it appears as if the objects are of a nature which we are not able to identify in terms of natural phenomena or commonly known man-made objects.

2. There is no indication of what kind of objects could have caused the images except that they must be of a construction, design, and material not commonly known. This is indicated by the computed acceleration rate and elocity (answer 8). For the same reasons, birds, aircraft and balloons are ruled out.

3. An analysis of the charts relative to movement indicate that there were group and individual movement. Within a group it appears as if the individual objects were moving counter-clock-wise along an elliptical or similar track. Thus when two objects crossed the camera line of sight they will appear to fuse into one. As they continued along their paths it will appear as if one object became two. This occured at reglar intervals at approximately every 25th frame as plotted in charts 5a and 5b.

5. The shape of the objects appears to be oblate or disk shaped, color; blue-white, and maximum and minimum size; 98 and 16 feet. The size is based on the assumption that the objects are five miles from the observer.

6. Fade in and fade out of the objects were analyzed as in 3 above. In this case the group movement was such that the distance between the objects and camera was increased so that the objects could not be recorded on the film thereby causing the apparent fade-out. Fade-in as attributed to a shortening of the distance from the fade-out area to the camera station.

7. Plots of the groups indicate that the objects move counter-clock-wise relative to the axis of flight path. However, nothing has been detected which indicates motion of the individual objects about their own axis although this motion appears to be likely.

8. In determining the velocity of the objects three assumptions were made:

a. The camera was held steady during Part III of the film.

b. The objects were moving perpendicular to the optical axis, and

c. The objects were five miles from the camera.

It is obvious that (b) is a fallacy; however, this assumption will give the minimum velocity and the actual velocity is greater than computed. The assumption that the objects are five miles from the camera is an arbitrary one. However, based on the emulsion speed and focal length, an object 50 feet in diameter and five miles from the camera will be recorded on the film with sufficient resolution to identify major details of the object. It is felt that if these objects were closer than five miles at the time of recording, details would appear on the film.

4. Discussion.

During the study and investigation of the unidentified objects, the preliminary data uncovered were revealed to experts (with proper security clearance) in the fields of astronomy and physics. Although they presented certain natural phenomena theories to explain the cause of the objects under certain conditions they were not able to do so under the conditions during which the photography was taken, nor were they able to recognize these objects as man-made.

As to the results of the investigations being reported, no attempt was made to corroborate the opinions presented. Because of the lack of proper equipment, money and personnel, the investigation was limited. There are obvious tests which can be conducted to prove or disprove some of the findings presented. It is suggested that these be undertaken.

5. Reference (d) requests spectrophotometric analysis of the Utah film be made. Preliminary plan of test is underway.

REPORT AND ILLUSTRATION OF A FLYING SPHERE

Observation by Prof. G.B. SIAS - Via Armando Diaz 22, Sassari

TO THE UNITED STATES EMBASSY ACCREDITED TO THE ITALIAN GOVERNMENT

APPARITION OF A FLYING SPHERE

"On the 28th of August 1952, the following article of mine was published in Sassari in the local "Corriere dell'Isola" newspaper:

"Yesterday evening, 27th of August, at 2145 hours, I was walking - as usual - along the court-yard of Sassari Brigade, below the windows of the war orphans dormitory, saying the rosary. It was exactly the time when the trumpet of Gonzaga barracks was playing the lights out signal. I watched now and then the sky covered with stars, heavy, moonless, still torrid for the temperature which in those days, as anyone would remember, often attained 40 degrees, with a sky which remained clean and cloudless for three months. Suddenly my attention was attracted by a transparent small cloud, coming from the East, isolated in the middle of the sky; the remaining sky was serene. My eyes were fixed to that point, fascinated by the view, when suddenly a sphere of astonishing brightness and luminosity seemed to depart from the Milky Way. I had the impression that it was very close to the earth; it was slightly larger than the full moon, of green-blue color, silver bright like the mother-of-pearl, with metal streaks in the right side; it proceeded at a dizzy speed along East-West direction, appearing suddenly as if it came out of a thick shadow. It came out and in a second disappeared, leaving behind a line or luminous ribbon, having a thickness of one-seventh of the sphere; after a second, the entire sphere appeared again; then again, it disappeared and the line showed and again the sphere returned, always identical. Finally, it disappeared toward the horizon. The apparition lasted in total three to five seconds.

"My first idea was that such a phenomenon was due to an aerolite. Everyone knows the color and brightness of meteoric stones, while it was evident that the luminosity of the sphere originated from the sun, like the moon's.

"In regard to motion, I reflected that such an object, suppose it was a human creation, could not have such a dizzy actual speed to excel the velocity of any human invention, even if carried to 50 or 60 kilometers altitude. On the supposition that the sphere was coming from astral spaces, from much higher altitudes, its motion could be either partially or entirely apparent, that is equal to the revolution speed of the earth, viz. thirty kilometers per second.

"Where the luminosity was concerned, I thought that it could be traced to the location of the sphere at hundreds or thousands kilometers above the earth while it got out of the cone of shadow of the earth and proceeded Westward, being illuminated by the sun which had set two hours and a half earlier. The location was the following: approx. 45 degrees between the Zenith and the horizon line, Southward; direction East-West beginning from the Milky Way.

"The doubt that mine may be a mere optical illusion is dissipated by the testimony of two other persons: an orphan, Brau, who had not yet gone to bed, saw the luminous sphere through the window of the dormitory; another testimony was offered by Mr. Piccolo, a guardian of Valmascheri concern placed approx. 3 kilometers in air line from Sassari, who observed the phenomenon at the same time: reality and not illusion, then.

ALTITUDE AND DIMENSIONS OF THE SPHERE

"The observation of the sphere, the peculiar circumstances of its apparition and the logical deductions, inspired me with a pressing desire, rather a stimulating impulse, to find a solution of the phenomenon in its complete significance. I had precise data:

(1) the small cloud which was a sort of signal
(2) the egress of the sphere from the earth's cone of shadow at 2145 hours
(3) the duration of the apparition for three to five seconds in South-West direction.
(4) the distance - cardinal point: South - of 45 degrees between the Zenith and the horizon line.
(5) the seeming diameter.

The sole thing to do was to contact a scientist: I went to Father Junkes, well-known astronomer, director of the Vatican observatory at Castel Gandolfo: after some days of study, he obtained with the system of the coordinates, the following results:

"On the basis of the geographical position of the observers, the coordinates can approx. be estimated as follows:

Longitude 33.8 East (08 degrees 33')
Latitude 40 degrees 45' North

On the basis of the sun position on the 27th of August at 2145 hours the resulting TMEC will be:

Aximuth 133 degrees 36' measuring from South to North, through West
Altitude 27 degrees 41', that is below the horizon

"On the basis of the above data, not taking into account the effects of refraction, the distance of the observer visibility in this point at an elevation of 45 up to the point where it comes out of the earth shadow is:

approx. 1681 kilometers Southward
approx. 1091 South-Westerward

At such a distance an apparent diameter of 1/2 degree (moon's apparent diameter) is equal to the following actual diameters:

14.67 kilometers at 1681 km. distance
9.25 kilometers at 1091 km. distance

From the above it can be easily deduced that the object observed could not be a common terrestrial "flying saucer", some bright metal body illuminated by the sun, because its dimensions would be too big."

These were the deductions of Father Junkes; but since he is also the Director of the Vatican observatory and well versed in astrophysics, he mentioned to me in another letter that the bright green, blue, silver colors and the luminosity of the sphere is presumably due to the remarkable quantity of iron and nickel which many astral bodies contain.

THE MYSTERY OF THE LINE AND SPHERE SHAPED LUMINOSITY

"Notwithstanding the numerous hypothesis which were advanced by the astronomer and myself in an attempt to explain such a phenomenon, none was entirely satisfactory. Still a quite reasonable hypothesis is that the discoid sphere, along its itinerary, presented to the sun alternately its surface entirely illuminated by the sun. Its dimensions were 1/7 of the sphere, that is two kilometers in breadth. This resulted in an undulatory motion, which was made necessary either by suspension stability in the space at that altitude or by some other equilibrium laws unknown to us.

PERSONAL REMARKS

(1) I must categorically affirm that the view of the sphere on my part was not casual; a small cloud, one cloud in a clean sky, which later on disappeared, was like a speaking signal to my attention. I dare not affirm - and it would be presumption on my part - that the sphere was occupied by non-human beings, no matter what they may be like: but the heavenly intervention is too evident!

(2) A luminosity which cannot even be compared with the brightness of full moon in a clear night; such bright and vivid colors that cannot be found on earth. All this was a heavenly smile which inspired my soul with a joy and peace never felt before. A new, heavenly light!

(3) I believe that privilege was not entirely intended for me: the phenomenon occurred in the Institute for War Orphans of the Sassari Brigade, the custodian of Trieste after the first liberation which waits for the second liberation from the hands of America, which is today the faithful custodian of it. I do not mean to get involved in politics, because I know nothing of it. I think, though, that this is a legitimate remark which reflects the psychology of history. America is based on freedom: freedom of thought, economical freedom, freedom of religion: in this connection, no other people in the world begins official ceremonies with the "Pater Noster" prayer: reflection of God wiseness and power! America defends freedom from fear: fear of war, fear of unemployment, fear of starvation. God put the destiny of the world in its hands. The oriental civilization elapsed, and so did the Greek civilization and the Roman world. The sacred Roman Empire collapsed, the British hegemony was eclipsed: the cycle from East to West is terminating in America. The words Virgilius wrote 2000 years ago, whom can better suit than America?

"Remember to rule the peoples with the authority of power: be clement to the humble and exhaust the arrogance of the superb" (Eneide 6th book)

The basic scientific data are here below briefly summarized.

(1) the certainty that the sphere is not a human invention in view of its dimension and heavenly light.
(2) the secret - now disclosed - of the measuring system of such apparitions
(3) the aim, resulting from astonishing revelation, of chosing a people as a guide to mankind, under the guidance of God.
The following is to be added:

(1) I intend to transfer the secret and the property of this writing of mine to the American Embassy, Office of the Air Forces.

UNIDENTIFIED OBJECT FLYING IN THE VICINITY OF PUERTO RICO
ON 16, 17, 18, 19, AND 24 NOVEMBER

1. On 19 November, the U. S. S. Gyatt picked up on its radar a contact tracking in excess of 3,800 knots. At this time the Gyatt was working an F-8 (Crusader) Fighter Aircraft at 35,000 feet when a high-altitude, high-speed object was detected. The object slowed and steadied down, maintaining a position to the fighter at nine o'clock, about nine miles from the Crusader. The Crusader pilot selected afterburner and attempted to close on the UFO. At about five miles, the object accelerated at extremely high speed in a 20° climb and pulled away from the fighter rapidly. The object appeared on Gyatt's radar for twenty-one minutes. On returning to Roosevelt Road's Naval Air Station, object again closed on the fighter from astern to four miles.

2. On 24 November, the Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range again held a high-speed, high-altitude target which simultaneously pulled away rapidly from another Crusader aircraft which at that time was flying at Mach . 99, 45,000 feet.

3. The Crusader pilot on the night of the 19th observed the UFO in full moonlight, weather was good and visibility was good. UFO was identified as a Delta shaped object about the size of a jet fighter.

4. The U. S. S. Gyatt confirmed radar tracks with motion pictures of radar scope presentation. The pilot estimated speed to be in excess of Mach 3.

5. ONI has no further information on this subject and we have requested that they notify us of similar incidents in the future.

6. For your information, the U. S. S. Gyatt is a Navy Surface-to-Air Missile Destroyer equipped with the latest and most accurate radars.

ATTACHMENT

SUMMARY:

This attachment outlines the exceptional circumstances and factors which dictate this officer's action in requesting voluntary retirement. 1/ It reviews his specialized experience in the development of physical security and allied equipment, which work has occupied most of his time since 1946 and has made him the governmental authority in this field.

It further describes the results of an informal unofficial survey he has just completed which accents the widely accepted need for improvement in our national industrial security program. In view of the recent abolishment of the Physical Security Equipment Agency of which he was the Director, the most expedient way to fill the need appears to be through the establishment of an independent civil organization working closely with the Office of Defense Mobilization and the Department of Defense. If this request is approved he intends to devote all of his efforts thereafter to this important task.

Ref. Para. 2.f. (PART II) Dept. Air Force Message, No. AFPMP-4BC ALMAJCOM 660/54 dtd 11 June 1954

1

Incl 1

BACKGROUND:

The decision to take this voluntary retirement action was taken only after the most thorough deliberation. It has been the most important one made by him in his entire military career, and it is also the most considered one, for he has been preoccupied with it ever since 4 March 1954 when a Department of Defense Directive abolished the Physical Security Equipment Agency (PSEA) of which he was the Director. He had been selected to head that Agency at its inception and served for the three years of its existence. During that time the Agency became the recognized authority within the government in the field of security equipment and it has an excellent record of unselfish service to the many agencies with which it was associated. He had also been serving as Chairman of the Federal Committee on Security Equipment since its organization in the fall of 1953.

Since 1946 this officer has devoted practically all of his efforts (about 20,000 hours) fighting Communism through technical means by developing security and investigative equipment. He consciously selected this specialized field of work in lieu of a conventional career in aeronautical Research and Development with full appreciation of the lack of opportunity for advancement in the more specialized field. He was firmly convinced that he could best serve the interests of

national security by such action. He realized that: - Just as a nation's organization for war depends on the technical weapons which are on hand - so does a nation's facilities security program depend on the technical security equipments which are available! It is estimated that less than 10% of the technical equipment considered necessary to implement a realistic facilities security program has been developed to date. We are in an advanced technological age yet our guard systems, both industrial and military, have changed little since biblical days!

As Deputy Commanding General (T-2 Intelligence), then Chief, Intelligence Department, Headquarters, Air Materiel Command, for the period December 1946 - August 1949, the undersigned managed a specialized laboratory known as the Science Survey Office (SSO) which developed certain classified types of security and investigative equipment. That laboratory was abolished for unknown reasons shortly after subject officer was transferred August 1949 to the Industrial College of the Armed Forces. From there he was assigned to the Central Intelligence Agency, leaving 1 March 1951 to become Director of the newly activated Physical Security Equipment Agency. Copies of pertinent directives are attached as Tabs A, B, and C. The need for such an activity as the SSO had continued to exist after its close-out in 1949. The advent of the Korean War so accentuated this need that the Management Committee, Office of the Secretary of Defense, after detailed deliberations, established

PSEA to ensure extension of the work of the earlier laboratory (SSO). PSEA was a joint project under the management control of the Department of the Air Force with the responsibility for providing for the development of physical security and related investigative equipment as a common service for all agencies of the Department of Defense.

It is estimated that PSEA had met only about 10% of its chartered responsibilities during its existence. There are several reasons for this state of performance; they include:

a. The initial small staff of 25 was never increased, as was planned, in proportion to the work-load that developed.

b. R&D funds for programmed activities were frozen as of March 1953 after less than two years of operation, the first funds not being made available until May 1951.

c. The Agency never operated under its revised Charter (Tab C) which would have insured full cooperation of the Military Services through the PSEA Policy Board.

The Agency's efforts concerning security equipment were just coming to fruition in the shape of a detailed R&D program, as the result of almost three years of background research work, when its untimely end came. Government agencies other than the Department of Defense which had come to depend almost solely on PSEA on physical security matters dealing with improved equipment included the GSA, State Department, AEC, NSA and CIA.

The matter of the Agency's continued existence had been under consideration by the Deputy Secretary of Defense since March 1953. The three Military Departments and the Office, Domestic Security Programs of OSD, all represented on the PSEA Policy Board, are on record as having supported the continuance of the Agency's activities, thus verifying the need for its services particularly in the security equipment field which constituted about 85% of its effort the last year of operations.

The Agency and its functions were abolished 4 March 1954 per Department of Defense Directive No. 5154.9 (Tab D). Although there was no stated reason, it is surmised that this action was intended in the interests of economy for it is understood that some other activities were stricken from the FY 1955 budget following the informal principle that any R&D activity would be dropped that did not directly support a weapon or weapons system already in or scheduled for production. This contradiction between the existing need for the Agency's services and the act of abolishing the Agency and its functions, leads to the conclusion that the Department of Defense does not consider the development of security equipment to be its responsibility. This apparently leaves the matter up to industry. This premise appears to be consistent with administrative policy.

THE NEED:

Assuming that the present policy of the Department of Defense in

regards to its industrial security program is limited to the statement of policies and principles, it is apparent that the most practical and sensible way to fill the void between policy and an adequate working security system in the defense industries is to follow the precedent of the Civil Defense and disaster control organizations and have the Government encourage the formation of an independent civil project in accordance with established principles of our competitive free-enterprise economy. Such a project would eventually be a large one and should preferably be a nonprofit organization of the highest standards in the tradition of Air Force Project RAND, the Battelle Memorial Institute and others.

It is believed that the importance of protecting our defense industry facilities (as well as our military installations) against sabotage does not require documentation here as it has been a subject of comment by the President of the United States, members of Congress, and other Government officials for some time. The Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation has stated to a Congressional Committee to the effect that the technical problems of his agency have increased ten-fold in the past one and one-half decades. In connection with Mr. Hoover's statement, there is substantial evidence that the USSR has spent an estimated 50 times more effort in the past 20 years than has been expended in this country on equipment matters associated with those of PSEA. It is noted that existing burglary protection systems of the

central station type are less than fifty percent effective in preventing
penetration of the protected areas by unskilled burglars. On the other
hand, protection against thoroughly trained saboteurs must be near
perfect because the saboteur can be considered to have accomplished
his mission once the penetration has been effected.

It is estimated that overall physical security in our key defense
industries can be improved in the order of four to five hundred per-
cent over a period of several years by the use of proper security
equipment and systems. The sums now being spent by the Depart-
ment of Defense for industrial and military security are described by
the Industrial Security Division (OSD) as "staggering" and are ex-
clusive of the security clearance program. The amount is classified
so it is not included here. A gain of several hundred percent in the
overall physical security of our Strategic Air Command bases should
be possible and would be of inestimable value. When it is considered
that it costs an average of $20,000.00 per year to man one guard post
in industry using civilian guards, and that military guards cost about
$40,000.00 per year per post, it appears possible to replace much of
this fallible human factor with advanced technological equipment with
a resulting gain in security, plus substantial savings in both money
and manpower. 1/

THE REMEDY:

During periods of leave since 4 March 1954, while acting unofficially
and solely as an individual, this officer has consulted informally with
representative industrialists and with casualty insurance and plant pro-
tection officials concerning industrial security problems and what an
individual such as himself might be able to accomplish were he retired
from active service. He has also talked with pertinent personnel within
the Department of Defense and Government and from this research has
established that there is a nation-wide need within our Defense industries
for the formation of an Industrial Security Engineering Service (ISES),
or the like, to serve the same purpose regarding protection against
sabotage as the various commercial Fire Protection services accom-
plish in regard to protection against fire. It has also been established
that no such service as an ISES now exists. The reaction to his pro-
posed solution to the problem has been most encouraging and has been
accepted informally as being soundly conceived in principle, operationally
practicable and economically justifiable. If properly implemented, it
has promise to fill a serious void in our industrial security program
which otherwise cannot be expected to be supplied for many years now
that the PSEA organization and functions have been abolished.

Subject officer is tentatively scheduled to be assigned in the near

8

future to Headquarters, Air Materiel Command, where presumably he
will engage in procurement work. His primary AFSC is Research and
Development Director (8416) with secondary AFSC - Staff Intelligence
Officer (2016). Including postgraduate schooling, he has served in
these categories for the past twenty years. Because of his experience,
subject officer considers himself to be the logical individual to under-
take such a civil project as outlined above and is willing to sacrifice
the almost certain security that continued military service would afford
in order to make the attempt.

He has the deepest and most sincere convictions that the best in-
terests of national security will be served if he is permitted to retire
from active military service to dedicate himself to serve a cause for
which he is most uniquely qualified.

CHARTER
Physical Security Equipment Agency

Pursuant to the authority vested in the Secretary of Defense by the National Security Act of 1947, as amended, there is hereby established, as a joint project under the management control of the Department of the Air Force, a Physical Security Equipment Agency (hereinafter called the "Agency") with the responsibility for providing for the development of physical security and related investigative equipment as a common service for all agencies of the Department of Defense.

I. DEFINITIONS

1. Physical security equipment is that used to provide warning of and protection against covert and other clandestine activities involving:

a. Military installations and their sensitive areas.

b. Materiel.

c. Classified documents.

d. Personnel.

This definition is not intended to preclude the Agency calling to the attention of elements of the Department of Defense applications of such equipment to other than covert or clandestine uses or to deny the services of the Agency to such elements in developing such equipment on request.

2. Investigative equipment is that required by the pertinent Department of Defense agencies for:

a. Criminal and related type investigative activities.

b. Counter-intelligence and counter-sabotage activities.

c. Intelligence activities.

II. DUTIES

Subject to the authority of the Secretary of Defense and in consonance with the requirements of the various agencies of the Department of Defense, the Agency shall perform the duties listed below:

1. For the solution of physical security and investigative problems, review pertinent basic and applied research and development projects and equipment, both domestic and foreign, and evaluate the feasibility of

modifying the equipment, or adapting the already demonstrated phenomena and principles. (Note: Foreign information and equipment will be procured through established Intelligence channels.)

2. Experimentally produce prototype physical security equipment:

a. Based on requirements furnished to the Agency by the various agencies of the Department of Defense.

b. Based on needs anticipated by the Agency.

3. Experimentally produce prototype investigative equipment:

a. Based on requirements furnished to the Agency by the various agencies of the Department of Defense.

b. Based on needs anticipated by the Agency.

4. When required by the various agencies of the Department of Defense, will with respect to specially developed equipment or supplies:

a. Procure service test quantities of prototype equipment and supplies.

b. Assist in the preparation of training and technical manuals.

c. Assist in training of personnel in the use of such equipment.

d. Assist in the maintenance of such equipment.

5. Furnish advice and assistance to other Government agencies on the above matters as appropriate.

6. Furnish, when requested, advice, assistance and coordination on matters concerning standardization, procurement, supply, operation and maintenance of the above items which may be adopted by one or more of the Services as items of standard issue.

7. Establish and maintain a working reference library pertinent to the mission.

8. Prepare an annual report on its activities for the Secretary of Defense and submit such interim program reports as may be advisable.

III. ADMINISTRATION

1. The Secretary of the Air Force, as Managing Agent for the Secretary of Defense, shall be responsible for the operations of the Agency and shall provide such personnel, facilities and other administrative services as may be required to insure its efficient operation.

2. The Secretary of the Air Force, with the concurrence of the other military secretaries and the approval of the Secretary of Defense, shall appoint a Director of the Agency. The Director of the Agency, if a military officer, shall be appointed for a term of three years and shall be eligible for one reappointment.

3. The Assistant Secretary of Defense (Comptroller) shall arrange with the three military departments for the financing of the Agency.

4. In view of the high technical, security and urgency aspects of this project, the Service managing the Agency shall provide all possible freedom of action in the conduct of operations of the Agency.

5. Each Service may assign such personnel to the Agency on temporary duty as may be required.

IV. RELATIONSHIPS

1. The Agency shall coordinate its efforts with all agencies within and outside the Department of Defense which have a mutual interest or responsibility with respect to any of its programs.

2. The Director and the staff of the Agency are authorized and expected to communicate directly and expeditiously with all agencies of the Department of Defense and appropriate sub-divisions thereof, concerning any matter within its jurisdiction and in which there exists a mutual interest or responsibility.

3. Services of the Agency shall be available to all Department of Defense agencies.

4. All agencies of the Department of Defense shall cooperate fully in assisting the Agency in the performance of its missions.

5. Each Service shall designate properly qualified personnel at appropriate echelons for liaison purposes.

SUBJECT: Letter of Appreciation

TO: Colonel H. M. McCoy
Chief, Intelligence Department
Headquarters, Air Materiel Command
Wright-Patterson Air Force Base
Dayton, Ohio

1. It is indeed a pleasure to transmit to you the attached copy of a letter of appreciation from the Director, Special Investigations, The Inspector General, United States Air Force.

2. I wish to add my appreciation to that already expressed for the excellent cooperation and assistance rendered by you and personnel under your jurisdiction in connection with the OSI Training Program.

3. It is desired that all personnel concerned, particularly Mr. Louis C. Gust, Mr. Guy B. Kidwell, II, and Mr. Earl A. Underhill be apprised of the correspondence and a copy thereof be made a matter of official record in their 201 file.

4. A copy of this correspondence has been made a matter of official record in your 201 file.

General Joseph T. McNarney

Dear General McNarney:

		On 11 March 1949, the first class of the Training School of the Office Special Investigations were graduated. During the course, important assistance was rendered by Colonel H. M. McCoy and Mr. Louis C. Gust of your headquarters. On 21 February 1949, Mr. Guy S. Kidwell, II and Mr. Earl A. Underhill of the Scientific Survey Office, Department of Intelligence, Headquarters Air Materiel Command, lectured to the class on "Sound Equipment" and "Investigative Photography."

		I should like to express my deep appreciation for the valuable aid and cooperation given by your command. The assistance of the above-named personnel contributed materially to the OSI Training Program.

				Sincerely,


		JOSEPH F. CARROLL
		Brigadier General, USAF

2. Your contribution to this annual meeting was of intense interest to all. You, Mr. Lewis C. Gust and all your staff showed throughout the presentation an admirable grasp of the technical advancements in your field of research. SUBJECT: Presentation by Colonel H. M. McCoy - 018054

TO: Commanding General
Air Materiel Command
Wright Field, Ohio


1. The Air University desires to express its sincere appreciation to Colonel H. M. McCoy for coming here on 28 April and addressing the faculty and students of the Air Command and Staff School on the subject of "Foreign Research and Development."

2. Colonel McCoy's excellent lecture was effectively illustrated through the use of well-selected motion pictures which added immeasurably to the students' comprehension of his subject. In addition to his formal presentation, Colonel McCoy very kindly consented to an extension of his presentation in order to permit a period of impromptu questions by the students from which they derived inestimable benefit.

3. The Commandant, faculty and students of the Air Command and Staff School join me in this expression of gratitude and appreciation for Colonel McCoy's outstanding contribution to our educational mission.

Daniel Guggenheim Aeronautical Laboratory

December 14, 1940

Subject: Course of Instruction in Aeronautical Engineering at the California Institute of Technoligy.

To: The Adjutant General (Through Channels).

1. The undersigned desires to explain in detail the course of instruction he is undertaking at the California Institute of Technology. It is requested that this letter be attached to his personnel file.

2. According to the provisions of Par. 44, Special Orders No. 131, W. D. Washington, 4 June, 1940, the undersigned started the summer course in aeronautical engineering July 15, 1940. He had previously in 1935 received the Master of Science degree in Aeronautical Engineering at this school. Upon entrance this past July he applied for and was admitted to Candidacy for Doctor of Philosophy Degree. Because the regular summer course was too limited for credits toward this latter degree; additional credits to total sixty-five (65) were taken and received for the summer term.

Upon detail here from the Materiel Division, Wright Field, Ohio, he had been directed by Bridadier General (Then Lieut. Col.) O. P. Echols to further perfect his knowledge of aircraft propellers, on which subject he has specialized the past six years. As there is no regular course in propellers, and as he has taken the majority of the aeronautical subjects during the year 1934-35 in addition to those subjects studied at the Air Corps Engineering School in 1935-36, it was decided with members of the faculty that the following schedule of subjects be undertaken. This schedule meets the requirements for credits for Candidacy for Ph. Degree and permit specialized study on propeller matters. It is noted that although admitted to Candidacy that requirements for Ph. Degree can only partially be met this school year. Hence no degree will be received. The schedule follows:-

1. Aeronautical Engineering Seminar. )
2. " " Research. ) (Scheduled course totaling
3. Aeronautical Mathematics Reading. ) 45 units.)
4. Technical German. (Regular attendance at this class. It is required that a test be passed for Ph. Degree but no credits are allowed Graduate Students for class attendance.)

The research problem item No. 2 is "The Control and Synchronization of Aircraft Propellers".

The Math Reading item No. 3 consists of regular attendance at four classes, auditing each for whatever pertinent information concerning propellers in particular and associated airplane problems that they may contain.

Advanced Problems in Airplane Design.
Elasticity Applied to Aeronautics.
Theoretical Aerodynamics.
Engineering Mathematical Physics (Vibrations).

In addition there is assigned and selective reading on vibrations, acoustics and advanced mathematics.

The above course entails a minimum of sixty-five hours of study weekly. Forty-five units of credits, however, are all that appear on the records forwarded to the Adjutant General. It was the desire to explain this that prompted this letter.

3. It is requested that if the above schedule, which was undertaken this first of three school terms, does not meet the approval of the office Chief of the Air Corps, or The Adjutant General, that the undersigned be notified prior to January 6, 1941, to enable him to undertake some different schedule during the last two terms.

s/ H. M. McCoy

H. M. McCoy

To:  Chief, Air Corps, Washington, D. C.

1.  It is recommended that Captain McCoy's schedule of study as given in basic letter be approved.  It is further recommended that he prepare, from original research, a thesis on the subject, "The Control and Synchronization of Aircraft Propellers," in meeting the partial requirements for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy.

2.  It is recommended that upon completion of this course, Captain McCoy be detailed to the Materiel Division, Wright Field, for duty in experimental research and development work on dual rotation propellers, propeller synchronizers, and hollow steel blades for propellers of large diameter.  He is considered to be an authority on aircraft propellers.  The Materiel Division is badly in need of officers with this specialty and no suitable reserve officers have been found, to date.

679th Company, CCC., Camp Goodar, South Branch, Michigan. August 16, 1933.
Subject; Special Report, 2d Lt. H. M. McCoy, A. C.
To; The District Commander, 3d Forestry District, Camp Silver Creek, East Tawas, Michigan.
1. I desire to make a special report on 2d Lieut. H. M. McCoy, Air Corps, on duty with this Company since July 17, 1933.
2. a. It might be expected that this Officer would voice some complaint at the difficulties of flying presented by his present duties. On the contrary he has showed initiative and enthusiam in adapting himself to his new assignment and adjusting his duties so that he can arrange to fly when it is possible.
b. With mostly voluntary labor he has constructed a very satisfactory emergency landing field.
c. As Mess Officer and Assistant Athletic Officer he has shown ability which I would rate as Excellent.
d. His initiative in relieving his superiors of work and his ability to plan and carry out new projects is Superior.
J. K. Colwell,
Major, Cavalry,
Commanding.

CITATION FOR THE BRONZE STAR MEDAL

HOWARD M. McCOY, 018054, Colonel, Army Air Forces, United States Army. For meritorious service in connection with military operations as Deputy Director of Technical Services, Headquarters, Air Technical Service Command in Europe from July 1944 to May 1945. During this period, Colonel McCoy performed outstanding services for the United States Army Air Forces by efficiently organizing, administering and coordinating the efforts of the several Army Air Forces activities concerned with the exploitation of enemy research and development activities. His membership on certain British Committees enabled him to obtain for interested American organizations the latest current information on research, developments and operations being conducted by the Germans on their V-1 and V-2 weapons. His services reflect the highest credit upon himself and the armed forces of the United States.
